selector.paragraph: Hemodynamically stable on admission with an unremarkable cardiac exam, the patient presented with lateral ST‐segment changes and elevated troponin‐T. Serial ECGs demonstrated persistent subtle lateral ST‐segment depression (< 0.5 mm in V5–V6; Figure 1). Initial labs were notable for HbA1c 5.7% and LDL‐C 142 mg/dL. Despite treatment with standard cardiovascular medications at the referring hospital, refractory angina accompanied by a rise in troponin T (8160 ng/L) led to the patient being classified as a very high‐risk NSTEMI profile. Furthermore, he was identified as a candidate for an immediate invasive strategy with CAG within 2 h (Table 1). The angiogram showed acute thrombotic occlusion at the ostium of the left PDA in the setting of a left‐dominant coronary circulation, resulting in extensive IPMI (Figure 2A,B). The hyperdominant‐LCx, which was widely patent and free of significant stenosis, supplied myocardial territories that are typically perfused by the right coronary artery (RCA) (Figure 2C). Additionally, the left anterior descending artery (LAD) showed two moderate atherosclerotic plaques (~50% stenosis) at the proximal and middle segments, which could potentially contribute to the subtle, non‐dynamic, STD observed in the lateral precordial leads (Figure 2C). The RCA revealed multiple proximal concentric stenoses; however, as it was not the infarct‐related artery, no emergent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) was performed (Figure 2D).

selector.paragraph: A 36-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of low-grade fever and severe stabbing headaches. Her past medical history was unremarkable. Neurological examination was unremarkable except for marked meningeal signs. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the head revealed no abnormalities. CSF analysis demonstrated inflammatory findings with lymphocytic pleocytosis (183 cells/µL; 97.8% lymphocytes) and elevated protein concentration (83.3 mg/dL). CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing did not identify an infectious etiology. Serological testing for tick-borne infections, including Borrelia burgdorferi, was negative. Based on the clinical presentation and initial laboratory findings, the patient was initially diagnosed with lymphocytic meningitis syndrome. She received intravenous dexamethasone (Dexaven) for 9 days, starting at 8 mg/day for 2 days, followed by 12 mg/day for 3 days, then tapered to 8 mg/day for 3 days and 4 mg/day on the final day, together with symptomatic treatment. A follow-up lumbar puncture showed partial improvement, with a WBC count of 130 cells/µL and protein concentration of 46.1 mg/dL. After 12 days of hospitalization, she was discharged in good condition on 11 March 2026.

selector.paragraph: At a follow-up visit on September 30, 2020, the patient reported progressive enlargement of the visual obscuration in her left eye since the day following her initial presentation. BCVA remained 0.8 in the right eye but had deteriorated to hand motions at 60 cm in the left eye. Blood pressure (BP) was markedly elevated at 187/104 mmHg, although she denied symptoms suggestive of hypertensive emergency, including headache, dizziness, nausea, or chest pain. Slit-lamp biomicroscopic examination with a fundus lens disclosed mild vitreous hemorrhage and expansion of the subretinal hemorrhage, while repeat OCT demonstrated progressive worsening of the neurosensory retinal elevation with accumulating subretinal blood components in the left eye (Figure 2). Given the patient's refusal of intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy, systemic antihypertensive treatment was initiated with oral nifedipine controlled-release tablets (30 mg twice daily) and metoprolol succinate sustained-release tablets (47.5 mg once daily), and she was instructed to maintain strict bed rest to minimize the risk of further hemorrhage.

selector.paragraph: A 74-year-old gentleman presented to the emergency department with an acute onset of weakness involving both upper and lower limbs, accompanied by exertional chest pain and discomfort. He had a history of a fall at home due to dizziness. ECG showed anterolateral ischemia, and the troponin T level was 313. Echocardiography showed global hypokinesia of the left ventricle and regional wall motion abnormalities, with an ejection fraction of 45%. Coronary angiography demonstrated severe triple-vessel coronary artery disease (Figures 1, 2), and a diagnosis of ACS with NSTEMI was established. The patient was managed medically with heparin 5000 units (injection), a diuretic, and aspirin (tablet). Revascularization was not beneficial as the coronary arteries were thin and completely occluded.

selector.paragraph: A 47‐year‐old female with a history of recent dental extractions of sixteen decayed teeth presented with one week of left facial numbness and swelling. She noted that the onset of her left facial numbness preceded her dental extractions by five days. Vital signs included a temperature of 98.2°F, blood pressure of 157/78 mmHg, heart rate of 78 bpm, and respiratory rate of 18 breaths/minute. On examination, she was in no acute distress and appeared nontoxic. Oral examination revealed left mandibular swelling, abnormal dentition with dental tenderness, and gingival swelling. Neurological examination was notable for reduced sensation to light touch in the left V1‐V2 region. Computed tomography (CT) of the head without contrast demonstrated hypodensities in the right parietal and occipital lobes. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with and without contrast demonstrated an 11 × 18 mm enhancing lesion in the right parieto‐occipital region with mild diffusion restriction and vasogenic edema, as well as small enhancing lesions in the right frontal and parietal lobes (Figures 1A–D). There were no paramagnetic rim lesions or central vein signs. Given the patient’s history of extensive dental caries, there was a high concern for odontogenic brain abscesses due to spread from her dental infections, for which she received empiric antibiotic treatment with IV vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and metronidazole. Infectious workup was unrevealing, with negative blood cultures, serum QuantiFERON‐TB Gold test, nonreactive rapid plasma reagin (RPR), HIV screen, and cryptococcal antigen. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no signs of occult malignancy, and the patient was up to date with her cancer screenings. A timeline of the patient’s clinical course is depicted in Table 1.

Multiple views of abdominal radiographs were done, showcasing a radiopaque needlelike structure in the right side of the abdomen and paravertebral planes, suspicious for a foreign body (Figure 1).
